extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors (especially those teaching transition-to-proof courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observable behaviors for validating student-written mathematical proofs; empirical study of how undergraduates read, make sense of, and judge the correctness of proofs after a transition-to-proof course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proof validation (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validation is the reading of, and reflection on, proofs to determine their correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selden & Selden: "A validation is often much longer and more complex than the written proof ... Validation can include asking and answering questions, assenting to claims, constructing subproofs, remembering or finding and interpreting other theorems and definitions, complying with instructions (e.g., to consider or name something), and conscious (but probably nonverbal) feelings of rightness or wrongness. Proof validation can also include the production of a new text — a validator-constructed modification of the written argument — that might include additional calculations, expansions of definitions, or constructions of subproofs. Towards the end of a validation ... contractions of the argument might be undertaken." (quoted text used as guidance and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of overall structure / proof framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the global/top-level logical structure to determine whether the attempted proof, if correct, actually proves the stated theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof framework is "a representation of the 'top level' logical structure of a proof... rich enough to allow the reconstruction of the statement being proved." In practice: write hypotheses at top, leave blank for details, and write conclusion at bottom. Lack of an explicit framework was noted by 87.5% of participants as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful line-by-line reading to check warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Read proofs line-by-line to determine whether individual assertions are warranted, explicitly or implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line-by-line checking is useful to determine whether logical implications can be justified; observed as common participant behavior and recommended for catching unwarranted steps or hidden assumptions (Weber & Alcock, 2005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking computations and algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify algebraic manipulations and calculations within the proof (e.g., expanding/binomial FOIL, factoring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed behavior: "Checked the algebra, for example, by 'foiling' (3n+1)^2" (62.5% of participants). Useful for detecting computational errors that may be fixable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing with concrete examples / substituting numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute concrete numbers for variables to test equalities or claims and to gain intuition about the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed in 37.5% of participants; recommended as a validation strategy for detecting false claims or misused forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rereading / multiple passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reread the entire proof or parts of it as many times as needed to make sense of the argument and to verify correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed in 87.5% of participants; rereading helps when initial line-by-line reading yields unwarranted implications or when constructing a situation model of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of focus/reflection aids (marking, pointing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physically underline, circle, or point to parts of a proof to maintain focus and highlight important phrases/steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed in 100% (underlining/circling) and 50% (pointing) of participants; considered beneficial for attention and as an aid to constructing understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting background/contextual facts or known results
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult definitions, theorem lists, or other context to determine which prior results may be assumed and whether gaps can be filled by known theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants consulted a provided Fact Sheet (56.25%) and sometimes questioned what the author of the proof attempt was allowed to assume. Example: recognizing that "if p is prime and p|ab then p|a or p|b" would fill a gap in a student attempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check exhaustiveness and relevance of case analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs use case division, check that the cases are relevant to the theorem and that the division is exhaustive and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: using odd/even cases to reason about multiples of 3 is irrelevant; participants failed to comment on such irrelevant divisions in some instances. Guidance: make role of cases explicit and ensure they bear on the stated conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and evaluating gaps in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify logical gaps and judge whether they are critical (invalidating) or minor/fixable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Proof (c)' had a gap; some mathematicians would fill it using a known result. Guidance: determine whether a gap can be filled by reasonable, accessible assumptions or prior results; treat easily fixable minor mistakes differently than structural gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing what is proved from what is intended (proves stated theorem vs other theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that the argument establishes the stated theorem rather than the converse or some other related claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Proof (d)' began with the conclusion and proved the converse; validators should check that the proof's goal matches the theorem's statement rather than a different claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, style, and notation consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess clarity of exposition, use of consistent and standard notation, and whether the writing 'makes sense' and is not 'confusing' or 'convoluted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants frequently objected to 'wacky' notation or confusing presentation (68.75% mentioned lack of clarity). Guidance: clear notation and organized presentation facilitate validation and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency without excess and appropriate level of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the proof includes enough information (but not extraneous material) to justify claims and to be convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants complained about 'too much, or too little, information'; e.g., not enough evidence for a contradiction in a purported proof-by-contradiction. Balance is required: avoid missing warrants and avoid irrelevant material that obscures logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subproofs / expanding implicit steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct small subproofs or expand terse steps to test their validity and to make implicit warrants explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All participants reported expanding proofs by making calculations or subproofs; this is a recommended validation behavior for handling compressed student-written steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings of understanding ('it makes sense') as a heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a cognitive feeling of understanding or rightness as a heuristic for judging correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 62.5% of participants said they tell if a proof is correct by whether it 'makes sense' or they 'understand it.' Authors caution this heuristic must be informed by experience, because some correct proofs may appear confusing and some incorrect proofs may seem sensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate validity from qualitative features (proof evaluation beyond validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the binary question of validity (does the proof guarantee the theorem?) from broader evaluative dimensions like clarity, insight, convincingness, and enhancement of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pfeiffer's notion: "determining whether a proof is correct... and also how good it is regarding ... clarity, context, sufficiency without excess, insight, convincingness or enhancement of understanding." Teaching should help students make this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranted implications assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claimed logical implications in the argument are warranted (i.e., the move from one assertion to another is justified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weber & Alcock (2005) emphasized warranted implications; when a logical implication cannot be warranted on first reading, reread or reconstruct intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and handling of backward or circular reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect reasoning that starts from the conclusion and works backward (which may prove the converse or be circular) and judge its admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Proof (d)' starts with the conclusion and arrives at the hypothesis; validators should flag proofs that appear to derive assumptions from conclusions rather than deduce the conclusion from hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of assessment items for proof comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess comprehension by tasks such as: rewrite the statement in your own words, identify the proof framework, make explicit an implicit warrant, and provide a summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mejia-Ramos et al. (2012) assessment model offers concrete items useful as rubric elements for measuring proof comprehension (and as precursors to deeper evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional recommendation: explicit validation training and formative rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach validation explicitly (e.g., through validation exercises, peer review, or rubrics) rather than assuming proof construction practice will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors conjecture that explicit instruction in validation is needed; cite Boyle & Byrne (2014) 'proof assessment tool' as a rubric used to help teachers give formative feedback and to structure peer comment activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/effort as indicators of validation thoroughness
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount of time spent validating a proof and the degree of engagement (e.g., number of rereads, amount of written scratch work) can be used as observable metrics of validation effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study measured min/max/mean validation times and noted long times (up to 25 minutes) as evidence of serious engagement; can be recorded as part of assessment of validation practices.
